ig_carousel_topic.topic: Hedging, when it's smart, when it's just buying back losses
ig_carousel_topic.slide1_text:
Should you hedge that bet?
Sometimes yes. Often no.
The answer matters more than you think.
ig_carousel_topic.slide2_text:
Most bettors hedge because they're scared.
A parlay is alive, the payout is big, and the last leg feels shaky.
So they buy the other side. Feels smart. Usually isn't.
ig_carousel_topic.slide3_text:
Hedging costs you expected value every time.
You placed the original bet because the edge was there.
Buying back against it means paying juice twice on the same game.
ig_carousel_topic.slide4_text:
When hedging actually makes sense:
- You locked +200 on a future months ago and the implied probability has flipped hard.
- A single win guarantees profit regardless of outcome.
- The hedge price is genuinely mispriced, not just comforting.
Example: $100 on a +700 future now at -300. Hedge $150 on the other side. Profit either way.
ig_carousel_topic.slide5_text:
The rule: hedge the math, not the anxiety.
If you can't show the hedge is profitable at expected value, you're just paying the book to feel better.
ig_carousel_topic.caption: Hedging feels like control. Sometimes it's just expensive fear. Know the difference before your next big leg cashes in. Save this breakdown.
